items.content: The city belonged to no one at that hour. Fog had settled into the streets like a held breath, softening the hard edges of buildings into pale suggestions, muffling the distant clatter of an early tram. She walked slowly, her footsteps swallowed by the damp air, past shuttered shopfronts and lone lamp posts burning amber halos into the grey. Everything felt borrowed — the quiet, the solitude, even herself — as though the morning had not yet decided to begin.

items.content: The velvet dark gathered around her like a held breath, the screen still blank and merciful. She had chosen the seat near the aisle out of old habit, though there was no one to disturb, no one to whisper apologies to as she shuffled past. The projector hummed somewhere behind the wall, preparing its small miracle, and she folded her coat across her lap and waited, grateful for a darkness that asked nothing of her yet.

items.content: The first step onto the beach always comes as a small shock, that ancient grit shifting and yielding beneath your weight like something half-remembered. Summer announces itself not in calendars but in this — the grains finding their way between your toes, warm on the surface and cool just beneath, carrying the mineral patience of a thousand winters. You pause without meaning to, letting the sensation travel up through you like a current, like the body recognizing something the mind had almost let go.
